qs.q: Why is sport good for children?
qs.a: Well, it keeps them healthy and teaches them teamwork. When a child plays football, he learns to cooperate, accept defeat and keep trying. For example, my nephew was shy until he joined a basketball club; now he has many friends. That said, sport should be fun, not a source of pressure.

qs.q: Should governments spend money on building sports facilities?
qs.a: I'd say yes, because accessible pitches and pools encourage people to be active, which reduces health costs later. For instance, a free public track in my town is full every evening. That said, the money must also reach schools and hospitals. On the whole, it's a sensible investment if planned well.

qs.q: Do you think professional athletes are paid too much?
qs.a: Well, it's a difficult question. Their careers are short and demanding, and clubs earn huge profits from them. However, compared with nurses or teachers, the gap seems unfair. For example, one footballer may earn in a week what a teacher earns in ten years. I'd say society's priorities are a little distorted.

qs.q: How does watching sport bring people together?
qs.a: It creates a shared emotion. Strangers hug when their team scores, and for ninety minutes differences disappear. For instance, whole neighbourhoods here gather in cafés to watch big matches and talk for days afterwards. That said, rivalry can sometimes turn aggressive. On the whole, though, I think it unites more than it divides.

qs.q: Why is it important to preserve traditional customs?
qs.a: Well, traditions connect us to our roots and give a community its identity. If we lose them, we lose part of our history. For example, the way my grandmother prepares couscous for celebrations brings the whole family together. That said, customs can evolve; they don't have to stay frozen in time.

qs.q: Do you think globalisation is making all cultures similar?
qs.a: To some extent, yes. You can find the same fast-food chains and films in almost every country. However, local cultures still survive, and some even gain pride by comparison. For example, young people in my area are returning to traditional music in modern styles. So I'd say cultures are mixing, not disappearing.

qs.q: Should museums be free for everyone?
qs.a: I'd say yes, or at least very cheap. Culture shouldn't depend on income. When museums are free, schoolchildren and families visit more often and learn naturally. For instance, a free museum day in my city attracted thousands. That said, museums need funding, so governments should cover the cost.

qs.q: How can young people be encouraged to take an interest in their heritage?
qs.a: Well, I think they respond to experiences rather than lectures. School trips to historical sites, storytelling events and short videos on social media can all work. For example, a local festival with crafts workshops attracted many teenagers in my town. So making heritage lively and interactive is the key.

qs.q: Why is scientific research important for society?
qs.a: Well, it solves real problems and improves daily life. Vaccines, clean water systems and mobile phones all began as research. For instance, studying viruses allowed doctors to stop deadly diseases. That said, results often take years, so governments must be patient. On the whole, I'd say research is the engine of progress.

qs.q: Should scientists be allowed to study anything they want?
qs.a: Mostly, yes, but with ethical limits. Freedom leads to discoveries nobody predicted. However, some experiments, such as those that harm people, must be controlled by committees. For example, medical trials need patient consent. So I'd say curiosity is valuable, but safety and respect for human beings come first.

qs.q: How can schools make science more interesting?
qs.a: I'd say through experiments and real-life examples. Reading about chemistry is dull, but seeing a colour change in a flask is exciting. For instance, my teacher once built a small volcano, and we all remembered the lesson. So hands-on activities, visits to labs and good questions make science memorable.

qs.q: Do you think people trust scientists enough?
qs.a: Not always, I'm afraid. Misleading posts online often make people doubt experts, especially about health. For example, some refused vaccines because of rumours. That said, scientists should explain their work in simple language. On the whole, trust grows when researchers are open and honest about uncertainty.

qs.q: Why is it difficult for adults to learn a new language?
qs.a: Well, adults have less free time and often feel embarrassed about making mistakes. Children just play and absorb the language. For example, my friend moved abroad at thirty and avoided speaking for months because he feared errors. That said, adults understand grammar better, so with regular practice they can progress.

qs.q: Is it necessary to live in a country to learn its language well?
qs.a: Not necessarily, although it helps. Living there forces you to use the language daily. However, today you can chat with natives online and watch films with subtitles. For instance, I know someone who reached a high level without leaving home. On the whole, motivation matters more than location.

qs.q: Should all children learn a foreign language at primary school?
qs.a: I think so, because young brains pick up sounds easily. Early learning also opens minds to other cultures. For example, children in some countries learn two languages from the age of six and speak confidently later. That said, lessons must be playful, with songs and games, not endless grammar tables.

qs.q: Will translation apps make language learning unnecessary?
qs.a: I doubt it. Apps are useful for quick help, but they can't capture tone, humour or cultural meaning. Moreover, speaking directly to someone builds a real relationship. For example, a business partner trusts you more if you try their language. So I'd say apps will assist us, not replace us.

qs.q: Why is it important for everyone to obey the law?
qs.a: Well, laws protect people's rights and keep society orderly. If everyone chose which rules to follow, there would be chaos. For example, imagine the roads if nobody respected traffic lights. That said, laws must be fair, otherwise people lose respect for them. So obeying and improving the law go together.

qs.q: Do you think punishments are effective in reducing crime?
qs.a: Partly. Clear punishments discourage some offenders, especially for serious crimes. However, they don't solve root causes like poverty or lack of education. For instance, a young man with no job may be tempted by crime whatever the penalty. I'd say prevention through opportunities works better alongside fair sentences.

qs.q: Should young offenders be treated differently from adults?
qs.a: Yes, I'd say so. Young people are still developing and can change with proper guidance. Sending them to adult prisons may make them worse. For example, a programme that placed teenagers in training workshops reduced repeat offences in one region. That said, serious crimes still need appropriate consequences.

qs.q: Why do some people lose trust in the justice system?
qs.a: Mainly because of delays and unequal treatment. If a case takes years, or the powerful seem to escape punishment, ordinary citizens feel hopeless. For instance, a neighbour waited six years for a simple property ruling. On the whole, speed, transparency and equality are essential to rebuild confidence.

qs.q: Why do some people take bribes?
qs.a: Well, I think it's a mix of greed, low salaries and weak controls. When someone believes they won't be caught, temptation grows. Also, if bribery seems normal, people copy it. For example, an official on a tiny wage might accept money to speed up a document. That said, it's still wrong and harms everybody.

qs.q: How does corruption affect ordinary citizens?
qs.a: It makes life more expensive and unfair. Money meant for hospitals or roads disappears, so services get worse. For instance, a bridge built with cheap materials because of dishonest contracts can collapse. On the whole, honest people pay the price, and trust in public institutions falls.

qs.q: Is honesty always the best policy?
qs.a: Generally, yes, because trust takes years to build and seconds to lose. A truthful person earns respect. That said, there are rare situations where kindness matters, such as not criticising a friend's cooking too harshly. For example, I'd always be honest in business, but gentle in personal matters.

qs.q: What can be done to reduce corruption?
qs.a: Well, transparency is the best tool. When contracts, budgets and decisions are published, it's harder to hide dishonest deals. Also, protecting whistleblowers encourages people to speak up. For example, a public website listing all tenders lets citizens check prices. On the whole, strong laws plus an informed public make a big difference.

qs.q: In what ways can artificial intelligence help in daily life?
qs.a: Well, it can save time on routine tasks. For example, a navigation app suggests the fastest route, and a translation tool helps you read a foreign website instantly. In healthcare, it can help doctors spot problems in scans. On the whole, it's like a helpful assistant, as long as humans make the final decisions.

qs.q: Do you think AI will take away many jobs?
qs.a: Some, yes, especially repetitive ones, such as data entry. However, new jobs will appear, like AI trainers and technicians. History shows this pattern: when machines arrived in factories, people moved to different roles. That said, workers will need retraining, so governments should support them with courses and guidance.

qs.q: Can we trust decisions made by AI?
qs.a: With caution, I'd say. AI learns from data, and if the data is biased, the decisions will be too. For instance, a hiring programme once favoured one group simply because past employees were similar. So humans should check important decisions and explain how the system reached them.

qs.q: Should children be taught about AI at school?
qs.a: Yes, I believe so. They will grow up surrounded by it, so they should understand what it can and can't do. For example, a lesson on spotting a fake image created by AI would be very useful. That said, basic skills like reading and critical thinking must remain the foundation.

qs.q: Why is privacy important to people?
qs.a: Well, it gives us freedom to be ourselves without being judged or watched. If everyone could read your messages, you'd feel uncomfortable. Privacy also protects us from fraud. For example, if a stranger knows your address and bank details, they can cause real harm. So it's a basic part of dignity and safety.

qs.q: Do you think people share too much personal information online?
qs.a: Yes, quite often. People post photos of their homes, holidays and children without thinking who might see them. For instance, announcing a long trip online can tell thieves your house is empty. That said, sharing is fun. On the whole, we should check privacy settings and think before posting.

qs.q: Is it acceptable for companies to collect data about their customers?
qs.a: Only if they are open about it and customers agree. Data can improve services, for example by suggesting useful products. However, secretly selling it is wrong. I'd say clear rules and fines are necessary. On the whole, people should be able to see and delete the information held about them.

qs.q: Should the government be allowed to use cameras in public places?
qs.a: I'd say yes in busy areas, because cameras can help to prevent and solve crimes. For instance, footage once helped police find a stolen car quickly. That said, there must be strict rules about who views the recordings and for how long. Otherwise, it becomes surveillance rather than protection.

qs.q: To what extent are good leaders born rather than made?
qs.a: I'd argue that leadership is largely developed. Some people have natural charisma, certainly, but it isn't enough on its own. Skills such as listening, delegating and staying calm under pressure can be trained. For example, many successful managers started out as shy employees and improved through mentoring. So talent may start the journey, yet experience shapes the leader.

qs.q: How does leadership in a small team differ from leadership in a large organisation?
qs.a: Well, in a small team, a leader can know everyone personally and adjust quickly. In a large organisation, communication becomes more formal, and a leader relies on managers to carry the vision. That said, the principle is the same: people must trust you. For instance, a clear mission statement helps thousands of staff move in one direction.

qs.q: Is it more important for a leader to be respected or liked?
qs.a: Ideally both, but if I had to choose, I'd say respected. A leader who is merely popular may avoid hard decisions, whereas a respected one acts fairly even when it is unpopular. For example, a headteacher who enforces rules consistently eventually earns affection too. So respect tends to produce genuine, lasting goodwill.

qs.q: What might happen to a country whose leaders lack integrity?
qs.a: The consequences could be severe. Public money may be misused, institutions weakened, and citizens could lose faith in any official promise. Over time, talented people might emigrate, and investors would hesitate. For instance, projects awarded through favouritism are often poorly built. Ultimately, integrity at the top sets the moral tone for the whole society.

qs.q: What are the biggest pressures facing young people today compared with a generation ago?
qs.a: I'd say the combination of economic uncertainty and constant online comparison. Previously, a degree almost guaranteed a stable job; now graduates may wait years for one. Meanwhile, social media encourages them to measure their lives against polished images. For instance, many young people feel they are falling behind simply because a peer posts a success story.

qs.q: Do you think young people are less patient than older generations?
qs.a: Perhaps, although it's a generalisation. Technology has taught them to expect instant answers, from messages to deliveries. That said, many young people show remarkable patience when learning skills like coding or music. So it may be less about age and more about the environment, which rewards speed in certain areas.

qs.q: How can societies make better use of young people's energy and ideas?
qs.a: Well, by giving them real responsibility rather than token roles. Youth councils, paid internships and start-up funding would allow fresh ideas to be tested. For example, a student-designed recycling scheme could be piloted in a district. On the whole, if we treat young people as partners, society benefits from their creativity.

qs.q: Would it be a good idea to lower the voting age?
qs.a: It's debatable. Supporters argue that decisions about education and climate affect the young most, so they deserve a voice. Critics worry about maturity. On balance, I'd lean towards allowing it, provided schools teach civic education first. For example, pupils who debate local issues in class would arguably be well prepared.
